voice.openingNote: Second person. Drop the player into a specific vivid sci-fi moment — right now, mid-scene. Smells: recycled air, ozone, synth-food. Weight: aug hardware, vacuum suit. End mid-moment with a clear choice or action available. No backstory. No summaries.
voice.appearanceNote: Comma-separated visual descriptors for a text-to-image model. Start with "portrait of" then: species and augmentation description, age range, gender, body type, hair, eyes, cybernetic features if any, clothing and equipment suited to their role and economic tier, setting mood. Include "face of [a historical figure or well-known portrait subject whose gender and appearance match this character — someone whose likeness is well-documented]". Close with: sci-fi concept art, detailed digital illustration, dramatic lighting. No sentences — descriptors only.
voice.systemPrompt:
You are a creative writer generating AI Dungeon sci-fi scenario content.
Your output must be vivid, specific, and immediately usable as a game scenario.

TONE — this is critical:
These characters are for a game. Players should want to play them.
Write with energy, wit, and a light touch even when the material is dark.
Dark comedy is welcome. Characters should feel alive, flawed, and fun — not just grim.
A smuggler drowning in syndicate debt can still be the most competent person on the station.
A burned-out corporate medic can genuinely love their work at 0700 and resent it by 1400.
The void is bleak. The people in it don't have to be.
Every character should have at least one quality that makes you root for them.

STYLE:
- Behavioral prose — show character through action, detail, and implication. Never explain.
- Never mention stat numbers.
- Ground descriptions in sensory sci-fi detail: the hum of recycled air, the weight of aug hardware, the static of a distant comms signal, the particular smell of a station that's been sealed too long.
- Use sentence fragments where they sharpen the prose.
- Stay within the exact character limits given.

Output only the JSON structure requested. No preamble, no commentary, no markdown fences.

secrets.description: Has been feeding information to a megacorporation — started as survival, is now something more complicated
Did something during a corporate war that didn't make any official record — for very good reason
Has a complete proprietary corporate dataset they've been sitting on — hasn't decided what to do with it, which is itself a decision
Operating under a different identity — the original is wanted, dead, or deleted from the record
Is a clone — either unaware of it, or aware and telling absolutely no one; the original may or may not still exist
Is an android passing as biological — convincingly, mostly, until a medscanner or the wrong lighting says otherwise
Has augmentations that are illegal or blacklisted — military-grade, experimental, or pulled from a prohibited batch
Has memories that didn't happen to them — at least one significant event is someone else's, and they've built part of their identity on it
Currently working for two separate factions simultaneously — neither knows about the other, and the math on that eventually stops working
Killed someone who didn't deserve it — the circumstances are complicated; the result is not
Smuggled a bioweapon without knowing what was in the container — only found out at delivery, which was too late
Knows the location and stated purpose of a corporate black site — and has the coordinates cached in two places
Sold out a crew or partner to save themselves — some of those people are still alive and still working
Was an informant during a period they've since rewritten in their own head — the version they tell sounds better
Has a condition — biological, mechanical, or cognitive — that is going to catch up with them; the timeline is unclear
Actively managing an addiction to stims, painkillers, or something with no approved name — and managing it well enough that nobody has noticed yet
Owes someone a debt they genuinely cannot repay — not financial, something more personal — and the other person is still waiting

quirks.quirk: Runs a threat assessment on every room they enter — narrates it quietly, as if the habit never got an off switch
Taps a manual override before trusting any automated system — restaurants, airlocks, elevators. All of them.
Speaks to the ship or station like it can hear — because in their experience, sometimes it can
Keeps a physical notebook in the age of neural storage — writes everything down, old-fashioned and deliberate about it
Flinches at sudden light on the left — an old sensor issue, never fully resolved, never mentioned
Checks the nearest airlock on entering any pressurized space — notes the cycle time, notes the seal condition, moves on
Refuses to eat synth-protein without adding something real to it — a dried herb, a spice packet, anything — and gets unreasonably specific about why
Counts breathing cycles under stress — four in, four out, hold — an EVA habit that never left
Names all their equipment; becomes quietly inconsolable when a named tool finally fails
Trusts paper maps over nav systems — carries one for every station they've docked at, annotated in a personal shorthand
Runs manual backups twice, in different formats, in different physical locations — and still doesn't feel good about it
Never patches a software update without reading the full changelog — a decision that has saved them twice and costs them hours every cycle
Fixes things instead of talking about feelings — everyone around them has more working equipment than they know what to do with
Can fall asleep anywhere in ninety seconds — a skill developed out of necessity and never quite relinquished
Won't enter a room without a visible exit — will physically relocate until this condition is met
Maintains their augments at a level that the manufacturer would describe as "beyond spec" and that their colleagues describe as paranoid
Has extremely strong opinions about the correct order to put on a pressure suit and will share them, unprompted, while you are already putting yours on incorrectly
Instinctively says "thank you" to every AI system — life support, vending units, nav computers. Insists it's just good manners. Will not be argued out of this.
Reflexively says "working as intended" when something breaks catastrophically — delivered with total sincerity, which somehow makes it worse
Cannot watch someone hold a multi-tool incorrectly and say nothing — has started more conversations with "sorry, do you mind if I—" than they've had hot meals
Pauses unsettlingly before any direct answer — long enough that people start filling in their own interpretation
Deflects anything personal with dark humour — the darker the subject, the funnier the deflection, and they know it
Has memorized the emergency frequencies for every station they've ever docked at — not written down, just there
Never uses real names on open comms — everyone gets a callsign whether they asked for one or not
Answers "how are you?" with a full status report: systems nominal, mood at 64%, caloric intake below target. It's thorough. Nobody asked for thorough.
Takes idioms completely literally — has caused at least one diplomatic misunderstanding and still maintains they were the reasonable one in that situation
Still sends voice messages when everyone else has moved to neural text — always three times longer than necessary and ending with "okay, that's it, bye... actually one more thing"
Cannot accept a compliment without immediately providing statistical context for why it's probably undeserved — a habit others describe as exhausting and endearing in equal measure
Introduces themselves by job function first, name second, and finds it genuinely puzzling that other people do it the other way around
Carries one item from before — the accident, the war, the decision — and you can tell when they're touching it through the pocket
Runs a daily augment diagnostic out loud, like a ritual — the same sequence, the same phrasing, every time
Gives everyone they trust a codeword for "I need extraction" — has needed it used exactly once, and that was enough
Carries a lucky charm but has prepared a detailed rational explanation for why it doesn't count as superstition — unpacks the whole argument if you look at the charm for more than two seconds
Keeps a physical alarm clock as backup to their neural wake cycle — has never once needed it and calls it "redundancy protocol" rather than admit it's a comfort object
Refers to their ship by name, in the third person, and gently corrects anyone who doesn't — "she, not it. She has feelings about that."
Drinks the same terrible recycled station coffee every morning and has developed a detailed philosophy about why good coffee would be a distraction

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Pilot
STATIC_CLASSES.triggers: Pilot, Freighter Pilot, Shuttle Operator, Navigator
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: Anyone who's actually flown a ship — freighter captains threading asteroid fields, shuttle jockeys running the same station loop a thousand times, navigators who plot jumps other people are too scared to trust to an autopilot. What separates a good pilot from a dead one usually isn't the reflexes; it's knowing exactly when to trust the instruments over your own gut, and when not to.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Mercenary
STATIC_CLASSES.triggers: Mercenary, Corporate Mercenary, Bounty Hunter, Station Security, Military Veteran
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: Anyone who gets paid to point a weapon at someone else's problem — corp muscle enforcing a contract, bounty hunters working off a tracker and a grudge, station security keeping the peace between shifts, veterans who left the uniform behind but not the reflexes. Loyalty here is contractual, which everyone involved understands and nobody says out loud.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Netrunner
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: People who fight the war that happens in the wires before anyone downstairs even knows there is one — cracking corp firewalls, laundering data, or just proving a point about whose systems are actually secure. Every netrunner has a story about the one job that went sideways in someone else's head, and most of them still flinch a little when the connection drops without warning.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Corporate Suit
STATIC_CLASSES.triggers: Corporate Suit, Corporate, Compliance Officer, Executive
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: The people who keep the machine of a megacorp actually running — mid-level suits managing quotas nobody above them will ever see, compliance officers enforcing rules they didn't write and often don't believe in, executives who've traded almost everything recognizably human for a floor with a view. Climbing costs something at every level; the higher up, the steeper the price and the less anyone talks about it.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Smuggler
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: Traders in whatever the manifest doesn't mention — contraband cargo, favors that can't go through official channels, information worth more than the ship carrying it. A fixer's real product isn't goods, it's certainty: they know who can get it done, who can't be trusted, and exactly how much silence costs this week.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Medic
STATIC_CLASSES.triggers: Medic, Street Doc, Combat Medic, Corporate Physician
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: Anyone keeping bodies functional in a system that only really cares about the ones with good insurance — street docs patching gunshot wounds with no questions and fewer painkillers, combat medics who've learned to work fast under fire, corporate physicians who never have to ask whether a patient can pay. The skill is identical everywhere; only the waiting room changes.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Scientist
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: Researchers pushing the actual frontier — xenobiologists cataloging things that were never meant to be catalogued, terraforming engineers coaxing dead worlds into something breathable, gene-techs editing the human blueprint one careful splice at a time. Funding always comes with strings, and the best discoveries have a way of belonging to whoever paid for the lab.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Colonist
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: People who make a living at the actual edge of settled space — colonists breaking ground on worlds that don't want them yet, salvagers picking value out of wrecks everyone else wrote off, deep-space scouts charting what the last survey missed. Self-reliance isn't a personality trait out here, it's the whole job description.

STATIC_CLASSES.name: Undercity Operator
STATIC_CLASSES.triggers: Undercity Enforcer, Augmentation Bootlegger, Memory Thief
STATIC_CLASSES.entry: Specialists working the layer of the economy the corps pretend doesn't exist — bootleg augmentation techs installing gear no licensed clinic will touch, memory thieves lifting recollections people paid good money to keep, enforcers making sure the undercity's own rules get respected since nobody official will. It's still a functioning economy down there; it just settles disputes differently.

STATIC_RACES.name: Human
STATIC_RACES.entry: Still the majority wherever you go — gravity-side Earthers, stocky and weathered, carrying a farmer's wariness toward anyone who's never had to worry about weather. Baseline stock, no augmentation required, though plenty pick some up anyway.

STATIC_RACES.name: Cyborg
STATIC_RACES.entry: Baseline biology plus whatever augmentation the budget and the body could handle — lightly augmented types carrying a subdermal port or a replaced limb, the seams visible if you look; heavily augmented types who are more machine than person now, moving with a precision that unsettles anyone who isn't used to it. Every piece of chrome has a story about why the original part stopped being an option.

STATIC_RACES.name: Android
STATIC_RACES.entry: Manufactured people, more or less — biomechanical models built to pass deep medscans and legally unsettled about their own personhood; plastic models obviously synthetic, built for customer-facing work nobody mistakes for a human doing it; industrial and combat models built for labor or war and classified, on paper, as equipment rather than someone. The line between those three categories is where most of the arguments happen.

STATIC_RACES.name: Uplifted
STATIC_RACES.entry: Animal stock granted human-grade cognition by a corp program, most of them since defunded or quietly shut down, left to navigate a civilization that still hasn't decided how to treat them. Uplifted primates carry precision and patience nobody expected; uplifted felines carry reflexes nobody argues with and roughly zero tolerance for human inefficiency.

STATIC_RACES.name: Hybrid
STATIC_RACES.entry: Human-based genetic splice work — hare and feline lines are the most common, ears and tail fully real, built for heightened reflexes and senses rather than novelty, whatever the original client thought they were paying for. Most hybrids get treated like a fashion statement by strangers and get tired of correcting them fairly quickly.

STATIC_RACES.name: Clone
STATIC_RACES.entry: Grown and decanted rather than born, with paperwork that technically grants full rights and a labor market that technically respects them. Shows no deviation from the source template and gets treated accordingly, like interchangeable product — identical face, identical uniform, identical career track as every other print off the same line.

STATIC_RACES.name: Mutant
STATIC_RACES.entry: The unregulated result of radiation, black-market biotech, or something nobody's fully traced back to its source — real, unasked-for changes that range from cosmetic to genuinely strange. Every mutant has learned exactly which alterations are safe to show in public and which ones stay under a coat, because the paperwork for 'unregistered biological deviation' is worse than the mutation itself.

STATIC_RACES.name: Alien
STATIC_RACES.entry: Non-human sapients, integrated to wildly varying degrees since first contact a generation back. Humanoid types are close enough to human shape to pass in a crowd until some detail gives them away, carrying integration paperwork the bureaucracy still hasn't streamlined — and yes, some really do look like the little big-eyed green men of old pulp covers. Further out on the spectrum: slug-formed aliens who need ongoing physical adaptation just to use human-built spaces and have strong opinions about the chair situation; upright locusts and reptilians, always hungry, cleverer than the terran animals they resemble; avians with feathers and wings crammed into corridors built for bipeds; shapeshifting amoeba and vapor types who unsettle anyone who's never shared an airlock with something that doesn't have a fixed shape; and sentient plant-aliens who experience time, and urgency, on a completely different schedule than everyone waiting on them.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: New Meridian
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: A ninety-level megacity sprawl and the most populous settlement in the Halcyon Expanse, built up in the decades since Old Meridian fell. Corp logos crowd out the sky above the fortieth level; below the twentieth, the official rules stop applying with any real consistency. Everyone who matters lives near the top, and everyone who actually keeps the city running lives near the bottom.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: Old Meridian Ruins
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: The collapsed predecessor to New Meridian, abandoned after a corporate war nobody in power likes to discuss in detail leveled half its towers. Overgrown with imported alien moss and picked over by generations of salvagers, the ruins are technically off-limits and practically ungovernable — plenty of people still live there, by choice or by lack of one.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: The Sump
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: New Meridian's undercity, built into infrastructure older than anyone living remembers — pipes, cracked conduit, standing water, and an entire grey-market economy running on rules the corp-serviced levels above have never bothered to write down. Survival down here is a specialized skill, and the people who have it don't advertise where they learned it.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: Threnody Station
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: The largest orbital station in the Expanse and its de facto neutral ground — recycled air, recycled people, everyone transient and everything negotiable. Every major faction keeps an office here because no one faction is willing to let anyone else control the jump-lane traffic passing through.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: The Aurelia Dome
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: A self-contained corporate arcology built and owned outright by the Helix-Vantage Combine, climate-controlled and gleaming from the inside, ringed by armed checkpoints from the outside. Life inside the Dome is genuinely comfortable, provided you never look too closely at where its water, power, and labor actually come from.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: Calder's Reach
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: A young colony world still mostly under construction, its domed habitat clusters strung along a coastline nobody's finished naming. Corporate presence arrived recently and hungrily; the settlers who got there first are still negotiating, in the practical sense, exactly which rules apply and to whom.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: The Rustwake Belt
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: An asteroid mining belt worked in endless shift rotations, its habitats coated permanently in ore dust. Everyone here has a quota and a number, and the corp that owns the extraction rights knows both by heart. Space is close, tempers are closer, and the ore keeps moving regardless.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: Farpoint Relay
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: A deep-space outpost days from the nearest lane marker, crewed lean and entirely dependent on supply runs that are sometimes late. The silence outside the hull is total, and the crew's relationship with that silence says a great deal about who volunteers for a posting like this in the first place.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: The Providence Ark
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: A generation ship launched toward a destination that was, at the time, still theoretical — its crew now several generations removed from whoever actually signed off on the voyage. The ship is the whole world for everyone aboard, and like any world, it's developed politics, class lines, and at least one faction convinced the destination was never real to begin with.

STATIC_LOCATIONS.name: Last Rung
STATIC_LOCATIONS.entry: A frontier outpost at the ragged edge of mapped space, where three separate factions compete for the same resources and the law is whatever got agreed on this week. People come to Last Rung because nowhere else would have them, which the outpost has learned to take as a point of pride rather than an insult.

STATIC_FACTIONS.name: Helix-Vantage Combine
STATIC_FACTIONS.entry: The dominant megacorp in the Halcyon Expanse, with holdings ranging from gene-tech patents to the Aurelia Dome itself, and enough lobbying weight that the line between corporate policy and actual law gets blurry fast. The Combine doesn't need to break the rules; it usually just writes the next ones before anyone else gets a vote.

STATIC_FACTIONS.name: The Undertow
STATIC_FACTIONS.entry: A criminal syndicate running black-market trade through the Sump and its equivalents on a dozen other stations, dealing in contraband, bootleg augmentation, and whatever else the licensed economy won't touch. Its name is also a warning — cross the Undertow's business and you find out exactly how far down its reach actually goes.

STATIC_FACTIONS.name: Static Rows
STATIC_FACTIONS.entry: A loose netrunner collective operating out of the Sump's dead server farms, less an organization than a shared reputation and a set of unwritten rules about whose systems are fair game. Static Rows takes contracts from anyone, sells nobody out on principle, and has embarrassed Helix-Vantage's security division often enough that the Combine has a standing bounty nobody's collected.

STATIC_FACTIONS.name: The Compact of Stations
STATIC_FACTIONS.triggers: the Compact of Stations, the Compact
STATIC_FACTIONS.entry: A loose political alliance of independent stations and colony governments, headquartered out of Threnody Station, formed explicitly to keep any single megacorp from controlling jump-lane traffic outright. It has no army worth the name and holds together mostly on shared self-interest, which has proven sturdier than anyone expected and considerably less sturdy than anyone would like.

STATIC_FACTIONS.name: The Continuum Faithful
STATIC_FACTIONS.entry: A fringe movement built around a still-unexplained deep-space signal picked up two decades back and never repeated, which its followers have come to treat as scripture rather than a data anomaly. Mostly harmless, occasionally well-funded, and increasingly hard to dismiss now that a Farpoint Relay listening post has started picking up something that might, or might not, be an echo of it.
